name: Cross-asset trend following
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Persistent Cross-Asset Trends
caseLead: Major trends in equity, bond, currency and commodity prices can persist for months as central banks, governments and large investors adjust their positions gradually. Trends often reflect gradual changes in monetary policy and investor positioning, while geopolitical events and trade restrictions can shift growth and inflation expectations for extended periods.
caseRest: Sudden trend reversals can erase several weeks of gains in a matter of days. Losses are most likely when markets move sideways or when a central bank or government decision reverses a trend that has attracted heavy positioning. The strategy can therefore lag for long periods, and its protection in equity sell-offs depends on those sell-offs developing gradually rather than reversing quickly.
figNote: Each card shows how far the S&P 500 moved during the episode, over the period described in the text. Trend following earns from sustained moves in either direction, so the size of the move shows how much trend there was to follow.

events.title: Lehman collapse drives a long equity decline
events.text: The S&P 500 fell about 17% in October 2008 as credit markets froze after the failure of Lehman Brothers. The strategy gained because short equity and long Treasury positions were already in place and the trends continued for months.

events.title: Rescue measures reverse the crisis trends
events.text: From 9 March to the end of May 2009, the S&P 500 rose about 36% as government rescue measures stabilised the banks. The strategy lost because its short equity and long bond positions reversed together.

events.title: Covid sell-off reverses within weeks
events.text: The S&P 500 fell about 34% between 19 February and 23 March 2020 as Covid closures spread, before emergency Fed and government support started a rapid recovery. Results were mixed because short equity gains were partly offset by losses when markets reversed.

events.title: Fed rate rises start a year-long trend
events.text: From January to October 2022 the S&P 500 fell about 25% as the Fed raised rates to control inflation and bond prices fell with equities. The strategy gained because short bond and equity positions followed the move for most of the year.

events.title: Bank of Japan rate rise reverses carry positions
events.text: The S&P 500 fell about 8.5% between 16 July and 5 August 2024 after a Bank of Japan rate rise and weak US jobs data unwound yen-funded trades. The strategy lost because long equity and short yen positions reversed within days.

events.title: US tariffs reverse established trends
events.text: The S&P 500 fell about 19% from 19 February to 8 April 2025 as US tariffs cut growth forecasts, before a pause in tariffs prompted a rebound. The strategy lost because dollar and equity trends reversed within days.

instrument: Equity index, government bond, currency and commodity futures; about 40 markets; held for weeks to months
rules: Long when the 3-month and 12-month price trends both rise, short when both fall; positions reduced when volatility rises; trends measured on daily closes
costs: Estimated commissions, bid-ask spreads and futures roll costs deducted at each trade
constructionTitle: Strategy construction, from trend signals to volatility-scaled risk

legs.position: Long or short equity index futures
legs.instrument: S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50 and Nikkei 225 futures

legs.position: Long or short government bond futures
legs.instrument: US, German, UK and Japanese bond futures
Euro, yen, sterling and Australian dollar futures
Crude oil, gold, copper and wheat futures

size: Set to a 10% annualised volatility target
exit: Position closed when the 3-month trend changes direction
stop: Market position closed after a loss of 2% of portfolio value
marketWatch: Rehyn watches whether price trends point the same way across the four asset groups, because trends that agree in several markets tend to last longer. Realised volatility in bond and equity futures matters because it sets position size and the risk of a reversal. Central bank meetings, tariff decisions and elections are the events most likely to change an established trend at short notice.

favourable.heading: Gradual, persistent policy cycles
favourable.text: Interest rate cycles that unfold in steps favour the strategy because yields and currencies keep moving in one direction for many months. In 2022, successive Fed rate rises lifted the US dollar and pushed bond prices down in a steady trend that the strategy followed in both.

favourable.heading: Prolonged equity sell-offs
favourable.text: Equity declines that develop over weeks favour the strategy because it can sell equity futures and buy government bond futures as investors move into safer assets. In the 2008 financial crisis, this positioning produced large gains as the S&P 500 fell by more than half and Treasury yields declined.

favourable.heading: Supply-driven commodity moves
favourable.text: Supply disruptions favour the strategy because producers and consumers take months to adjust, so prices keep moving after the first reaction. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine pushed oil, gas and wheat prices higher for several months, which rewarded long positions.

adverse.heading: Sharp reversals after policy surprises
adverse.text: Policy surprises hurt the strategy when they reverse a trend that has attracted heavy positioning, leaving it on the wrong side of several markets at once. In August 2024, a Bank of Japan rate rise reversed long equity and short yen positions within days.

adverse.heading: Range-bound markets without direction
adverse.text: Markets that move sideways hurt the strategy because trend signals reverse repeatedly, so each new position loses a small amount through reversals and trading costs. Trend followers struggled in 2016 for this reason, as oil and equity prices reversed several times within the year.

adverse.heading: Rebounds after severe sell-offs
adverse.text: Sharp recoveries hurt the strategy because it holds short equity and long bond positions when markets turn upward. In March 2009, the S&P 500 began a rally of about 36% over three months, and the strategy lost on those defensive positions.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's peak-to-trough drawdown during each event, measured from its value just before the event to its lowest point using the default backtest parameters above. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in equity indices, bond yields, currencies and commodity prices, which are then applied to the strategy's current positions.
